segs.text: There is a book in a library in Connecticut that no one has been able to show how to read. Codebreakers, linguists and computers have worked on it for more than a century. This episode keeps three things apart: what is established about the book, what people have claimed, and what is still open.

The object. It is catalogued as Beinecke M S 408, and it belongs to the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale. About two hundred forty pages survive, out of an estimated two hundred seventy two, a figure reconstructed from gaps. It is handwritten on vellum, in a script Yale describes as unidentified, and illustrated with plants, star charts, and small figures that seem to be bathing. It is called the Voynich manuscript, after Wilfrid Voynich, the dealer who bought it in 1912.

Established: its age. In 2009, a team at the University of Arizona radiocarbon dated samples of the vellum and got a range of 1404 to 1438. That dates the animal skin, not the writing on it. Analyses of the ink and paints found materials consistent with the period. Together, these make a modern forgery difficult to argue.

Established: part of its history. The earliest known document that mentions it is a letter written in Prague in 1639 by Georg Baresch to the scholar Athanasius Kircher. A later letter, from Jan Marci in 1665 or 1666, passes on a story, told to Marci by a third person, that Emperor Rudolf the Second once paid six hundred ducats for the book, and that Roger Bacon wrote it. No independent record confirms it, and the Bacon idea is now largely discredited. Yale received the book in 1969, donated by the dealer H. P. Kraus.

Now the text, which is where the real puzzle lives. It runs to roughly one hundred seventy thousand characters, about thirty eight thousand transcribed words, with about eight thousand different forms. Counts vary between transcriptions, and a word here just means a string between spaces. The word frequencies follow a Zipf-like curve, the pattern found in natural languages, where a few words are very common and most are rare. Studies have also reported language-like patterns, such as related words clustering in related places. Patterns like these do not by themselves prove a language.

But it also behaves unlike the languages we can test. Claire Bowern and Luke Lindemann reviewed the evidence in 2021. On one measure of letter predictability, conditional entropy, they report about two bits for the text, lower than in their samples of natural languages. Some characters appear almost only at the start or end of words. Scholars label two varieties of the text, A and B, with different profiles, after Prescott Currier. And Lisa Fagin Davis has argued, from the handwriting, that five scribes worked on it.

Put those together and you have the central problem. To many researchers the text looks structured, yet no proposed reading has been broadly accepted. That describes the data. It is not an explanation.

Now the claims. Many people have announced a solution, so here is the pattern, with the best known cases. In 1921, William Newbold of the University of Pennsylvania said the pages hide a second script of microscopic shorthand. John Manly of the University of Chicago published a critique in 1931 that dismantled Newbold's readings. Newbold's readings were not accepted, and the idea is considered discredited.

Later claims. In 2013, Tucker and Talbert read it as Nahuatl, the Aztec language. In 2017, Nicholas Gibbs wrote in the Times Literary Supplement that it is abbreviated Latin about women's health. The same year, Greg Kondrak and Bradley Hauer proposed Hebrew with scrambled letters, using a computer method. In 2018, Ahmet Ardic said it was an old Turkic language. In 2019, Gerard Cheshire said it was a proto-Romance language. Each was reported or promoted as a solution.

Lisa Fagin Davis said Gibbs's method does not produce Latin that makes sense, and called Cheshire's method circular. The Nahuatl specialist M. Pharao Hansen called the Tucker and Talbert readings pure speculation. What the critiques share is this: the readings did not give text that independent specialists found coherent. A credible decipherment should be testable: others following its rules should get the same readable text, and it should predict pages nobody has read. None of the proposals here has met that standard.

Two other ideas deserve fairness. One is that it is a hoax, meaningless text made to look like writing. In 2003, Gordon Rugg showed that a table of word parts and a card with holes can generate text with some similar features. That shows a method is possible, not that it was used. In 2013, Marcelo Montemurro and Damian Zanette reported word patterns that they argued would be unlikely in a hoax. How much that proves is debated.

The other idea is a cipher. In 2025 the science journalist Michael Greshko published in the journal Cryptologia a method he calls the Naibbe cipher. Using procedures plausible for the fifteenth century, it turns ordinary Latin or Italian into text that reproduces some measured properties of the Voynich. He presents it as a proof that such a cipher could be built, not as a solution to the book. And in 2026, Layfield and Davis argued in Digital Medievalist that the pages were made as four-page units and bound out of order in the fifteenth century. If so, any analysis that depends on page order may be misled. Davis said we do not know if it is a code.

So what is open? Almost everything about meaning. A natural language in an invented script? A cipher? A constructed language? Meaningless text? Each has supporters, and none has proof. Who made it, where, and why are open, and so is what the baths and charts were for.

The ledger. Documented: the vellum dates to 1404 to 1438, the book was in Prague by 1639, and Yale holds it. Measured: language-like word statistics, low letter entropy, two text varieties, several hands. Claimed: every decipherment so far. Competing explanations: hoax, cipher, or language, with unequal support. Unknown: what it says, if anything, and who made it.

So can anyone read the book nobody can read? Not yet. Not established, and not ruled out. Yale has put scans online, free for anyone. A credible solution would produce coherent text that other people can reproduce.
